'''Ann Elizabeth Nelson''' (April 29, 1958 – August 4, 2019) was an American [[Particle physics|particle physicist]] and professor of physics in the Particle Theory Group at the [[University of Washington]] from 1994 until her death.<ref name="NewYorkTimes" /><ref name="SeattleTimes" /><ref name=Quanta190822/> Nelson received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 2004,<ref name=GuggenheimFellow /> and she was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2011<ref name=AmAcadDirectory /> and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2012.<ref name=NASDirectory /> She was a recipient of the 2018 [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics]], presented annually by the [[American Physical Society]] and considered one of the most prestigious prizes in physics.<ref name=SakuraiPrize />

== Education ==
Born in Baton Rouge, Louisiana,<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/08/26/science/ann-nelson-dies.html |title = Ann Nelson, Expert on Particle Physics, is Dead at 61|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 2019-08-26|last1 = McClain|first1 = Dylan Loeb}}</ref> Nelson earned her [[Bachelor of Science]] degree at [[Stanford University]] in 1980,<ref name=AIPProfile /> and her Ph.D. degree at [[Harvard University]] under the supervision of [[Howard Georgi]] in 1984.<ref name=HavardNewsletter2018 />

== Career ==
After a post doctoral fellowship at the [[Harvard Society of Fellows]] from 1984 to 1987, Nelson became an assistant professor at Stanford University in 1987. In 1990 Nelson moved to [[University of California, San Diego|UC San Diego]], and then in 1994 moved for the final time her career to the [[University of Washington]].<ref name = iNSPIREprof />

== Research ==
Nelson is known for a number of theories, including:

* The Nelson–Barr mechanism, a proposed solution to the [[strong CP problem]]. The theory was developed independently by Nelson and [[Stephen Barr]] in 1984.<ref name =NelsonBarr /> Nelson was a doctoral student at Harvard at the time.<ref name=Quanta190822 />
*The theory of spontaneous [[CP violation|violation of CP]] (charge conjugation and parity symmetry), which may explain the origin of the asymmetry observed between matter and anti-matter.<ref name =SpontaneousCPV />
* The theory of [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose–Einstein condensation]] of [[kaon]] mesons in dense matter, which predicts [[strangeness]] in [[neutron star]]s.<ref name=Kaons />
* The basic mechanism for [[Baryogenesis|electroweak baryogenesis]], which may explain the origin of matter in the universe.<ref name=EWBaryo />
* The theory of gauge-mediated [[supersymmetry breaking]], which accounts for how supersymmetry at short distances might be compatible with the absence of observed flavor-symmetry violation at long distances.<ref name=supersym />
* The [[little Higgs]] theory, which may explain why the Higgs boson must be relatively light.<ref name = LittleHiggs />
* The theory of "accelerons", which relates neutrino masses to the [[Dark energy|cosmological dark energy]] responsible for the relatively recent acceleration of the expansion of the universe.<ref name=PO040727 />

== Personal life ==
Nelson was married to [[David B. Kaplan]], also a professor of physics at the University of Washington. She had been an active member of [[The Mountaineers (club)|The Mountaineers]] club in Seattle since 1994. She had two children.<ref name=UW />

Nelson was an activist for equal rights throughout her life. In 1980, when graduating from Stanford University, she and her husband wore colored ribbons to protest Stanford's investments in [[Apartheid]] [[South Africa]]. In 2017, she led physics lectures in [[Palestinian territories|Palestine]] to support social justice and promote diversity in science fields around the world.<ref name=Quanta190822/> She advocated for greater [[Women in STEM fields|representation of women in physics research]].<ref name=PhysicsToday170501/>

===Death===
On August 4, 2019, while hiking [[Iron Cap Mountain]] in the [[Alpine Lakes Wilderness]] with her husband and two friends, Nelson lost her footing and died after falling into a rocky gully. Her husband and fellow hikers were rescued on August 4 by a [[Spokane County, Washington|Spokane]] helicopter crew. Her body was recovered on August 6.<ref name="SeattleTimes" /><ref name="Mountaineers" /><ref name=SM190808/>
